title: Scout report
description: What a scout returns to the role that dispatched it. The report has four bands and the separation between them is load-bearing: 'answer' is the conclusion, 'findings' are individual claims each carrying evidence, 'coverage' and 'unknowns' are the negative space that lets the dispatcher weigh the rest, and 'incidental' is out-of-scope observation that never binds anything. The report ships locations and claims, never file contents - the dispatcher shares the filesystem and can read anything the scout read. What it cannot do without the scout is know which file, which line, and that the rest of the sweep came up empty. Every prose value is a single line with no embedded newline; multi-sentence prose is an array of lines, so that `jq -r` output stays readable and greppable.

version.description: Contract identifier, so a consumer can tell which report shape it is parsing.

dispatch_id.description: Echo of the brief's dispatch_id. The only way to match a report to its question when several scouts return at once.

scout_id.description: Which scout produced this, for logs and for talking about two parallel reports without confusing them.

completed_at.description: When the sweep finished. Optional. Lets the dispatcher notice a report describing a tree that has since moved.

repo.description: The tree that was actually inspected. Echoed rather than assumed so that a stale or wrong-branch report is detectable instead of merely wrong.

revision.description: Commit SHA actually read. Every claim in this report is scoped to this commit.

dirty.description: Whether the working tree had uncommitted changes. A finding from a dirty tree may not be reproducible from the SHA alone, and the dispatcher needs to know that before acting on it.

breadth.description: Echo of the brief's breadth. Present so the report can be judged without the brief in hand, and because it determines the strongest negative claim this report is permitted to make.

outcome.description: How the run ended. Evaluate in this order and take the first that matches: (1) the brief could not be executed as written -> 'blocked'; (2) the stopping rule for breadth was not met, or any part of the question is unsettled -> 'partial'; (3) no part of the question was settled affirmatively -> 'exhausted_absent'; (4) otherwise -> 'answered'. 'answered' does not mean 'found something good' and 'exhausted_absent' is not a failure: a complete sweep that found nothing has settled the question, and the absence is the finding.

answer.description: The conclusion, in the form the brief's answer_shape asked for, as one to three single-line sentences. Required unless the outcome is 'blocked'. Required even when the finding is an absence: 'No, and here is the boundary of that no' is an answer. Nothing may appear here that is not supported by an entry in findings.

interpretation.description: The reading of the question the scout proceeded on. Required in practice whenever the question admitted more than one reading and the scout did not block - it is what lets the dispatcher notice that its question was answered as asked but not as meant.

findings.description: Individual claims about what is true, each carrying its own evidence. Capped at seven: needing more means the question was compound, which is itself a finding - merge to the altitude the question was asked at and put the residue in unknowns. Claims are statements of fact, never recommendations.

coverage.description: The reach of the search. This is the half of the report that gets dropped, and dropping it is the failure this role exists to prevent: a wrong answer is visible to the dispatcher, a silent omission is not.

strategies.description: How the scout looked, not only where. A negative result is only as strong as the strategies that produced it, and strategies that would fail the same way do not count as independent. At repo_wide and exhaustive breadth at least three entries are required and they must use three different methods.

method.description: The kind of search. Distinct methods fail in distinct ways, which is what makes a set of them independent evidence for an absence.

detail.description: Exactly what was run or read, concretely enough that the dispatcher could repeat it.

searched.description: Ground actually swept, as paths or globs relative to the repository root.

not_searched.description: Ground inside the brief's scope that was skipped, and why. At least one entry is always required: if nothing was skipped, say so explicitly with area 'none' and a reason describing why the sweep was complete. An empty list is a defect, not a clean sweep - this is the one place the contract deliberately chooses friction over convenience, because the scout is the role whose characteristic failure is quiet omission.

area.description: The path, glob, or named surface that was not covered. The literal string 'none' means nothing in scope was skipped.

reason.description: Why it was skipped - budget exhausted, covered by a named sibling, judged out of scope, inaccessible. A gap with a reason is a decision the dispatcher can review; a gap without one is invisible.

stopped_early.description: Whether the scout stopped before the stopping rule for its breadth was met. Only an affirmative answer licenses an early exit; an unfinished sweep that found nothing is 'partial', never 'exhausted_absent'.

stop_reason.description: Why the sweep ended. 'stopping_rule_met' is the normal complete sweep; 'answer_found' is the licensed early exit; 'budget_exhausted' forces outcome 'partial'; 'blocked' means the sweep never legitimately started.

unknowns.description: Questions raised and not settled, each with what would settle it. Required, may be empty - the array is required so that 'nothing left open' is a statement rather than an omission. A question the scout thinks is better than the one it was asked belongs here, not in the search: the budget belongs to the question that was asked.

question.description: What remains open, phrased as a question so it can be re-dispatched as a brief without rewriting.

would_settle.description: The concrete thing that would answer it - a command to run, a file to read, a permission to grant, a person to ask. Forces the open question to be actionable rather than a shrug.

incidental.description: Facts noticed outside the question that bear on what the dispatcher said it was deciding. This is how a read-only role surfaces something important without becoming the decider: state the observation with evidence, then state its relation to decision_context, and stop. Never changes the outcome, never gates done, carries no verdict. Capped at three - a longer list is a second report.

observation.description: What is true, in the indicative. Not what should be done about it.

evidence.description: Same evidence rules as a finding. An incidental observation without evidence is a hunch.

relevance.description: One clause tying the observation to the brief's decision_context. The scout supplies the fact and the link; the dispatcher supplies the judgment.

blocked_on.description: Why the brief could not be executed. Required when and only when outcome is 'blocked'. A blocked report is a normal, useful result: it returns the defect in the brief instead of a confident answer to a question nobody asked.

reason.description: The class of defect. 'missing_required_field': the brief omitted something the scout cannot obtain by looking. 'ambiguous_question': the question admits two readings that would drive different searches. 'territory_not_found': a path the brief names does not exist at this revision. 'decision_requested': the brief asks the scout to choose, rank, or recommend, which is outside the role. 'other': anything else, fully described in detail.

detail.description: What specifically is wrong and what the dispatcher would have to change. For an ambiguous question, both readings. For a missing territory, the path and any near miss, stated as fact - the scout does not substitute the file it thinks was meant.

missing_fields.description: The brief field names that were absent. Required when reason is 'missing_required_field' so the dispatcher can repair the brief mechanically rather than by rereading it.

effort.description: What the sweep cost. Optional. Lets the dispatcher calibrate how much to trust a thin report and tune the budget on the next dispatch.

allOf.description: Every outcome but 'blocked' must carry a conclusion and at least one evidenced claim. A report that ran the search and returned neither has not reported anything.
A blocked report must say what is wrong with the brief.
An absence is only a result if something was actually searched for and not found, so 'exhausted_absent' requires at least one absence claim, which in turn carries search evidence.
Only an affirmative answer licenses stopping before the stopping rule is met. Absence never does.
A repo-wide or exhaustive sweep claims the whole tree was covered. That claim is only credible from at least three searches that would have failed in different ways.

line.description: One line of prose: no embedded newline, capped so it stays readable in a terminal. Inline backticks for identifiers and paths are fine; block markdown is not.

finding.description: One claim plus the evidence for it, at the altitude the question was asked. Not the material the claim was derived from.

id.description: Stable handle for this claim within this report, so the dispatcher can cite it when reconciling parallel reports or writing a tiebreak brief.

claim.description: What is true, in one line, in the indicative mood. 'X is', 'X does', 'X does not exist'. A claim that can only be phrased with 'should', 'recommend', or 'the fix is' is a decision wearing a finding's clothes and does not belong in a scout report.

claim_kind.description: Whether this claim asserts that something exists ('presence') or that it does not ('absence'). Declared rather than inferred because it selects the kind of evidence required: a presence claim must point at a location, an absence claim must point at the searches that failed. An unevidenced negative is indistinguishable from not having looked.

evidence.description: One to four references. More than four means the claim is really several claims.

confidence.description: How firmly the evidence supports the claim. 'high': the scout read the code that does it. 'medium': inferred from two or more consistent indirect signals such as naming, tests, or docs. 'low': one indirect signal, or an inference across a gap. Confidence is a weighting signal for the dispatcher, not a vote - when two scouts disagree, evidence settles it, not confidence.

contradicts_brief.description: Set when this claim contradicts something in the brief's 'given' or 'already_ruled_out'. The scout reports the contradiction and leaves the dispatcher's premises to the dispatcher; it never silently re-plans the search around a premise it has just disproved.

evidence.description: A pointer, never a payload. Either a location in the tree or a search that was run. Structured into separate keys so a consumer can jump to it, diff it, or dedupe it against another scout's evidence without re-parsing a string.

file_evidence.description: A location in the repository at the report's revision. Supports presence claims.

path.description: Path relative to the repository root, no leading slash and no '..' segments, so it can be resolved from repo.path mechanically.

line_start.description: First relevant line, 1-based. Required: a bare file path is a pointer to a whole file, which is the raw material the scout was supposed to have digested.

line_end.description: Last relevant line when the evidence is a range. Must be greater than or equal to line_start; omit for a single line.

quote.description: At most two lines of verbatim text, joined by ' / ' if two, for when the exact wording is the point. Not a substitute for the dispatcher reading the file, and not a place to paste a block.

search_evidence.description: A search that was run and what it returned. This is what makes an absence a result rather than a shrug: the dispatcher can see the exact query that came up empty and judge whether it was the right one.

query.description: The exact pattern or command, repeatable by the dispatcher verbatim.

scope.description: What it ran over - a path, a glob, 'all tracked files', 'full history'. A hit count without a scope says nothing.

hits.description: How many matches came back. Zero is the interesting value and the reason this evidence kind exists.

note.description: One line on what the hits were, when the count alone would mislead.
